passage: Aparna, your cousin is shouting at the TV again, calling the other team cheats for the same tackle his team made. He reminds me of my brother Gopal. At our school in Madurai there were four houses, and Gopal was Green House, heart and soul. On sports day, when a Green runner stepped over the line, Gopal shouted, "Accident! The chalk was faded!" Ten minutes later a Blue boy did the same, and Gopal was on his feet: "Cheating! Disqualify him!" I was in Blue, so we fought all the way home. Amma laughed and said, "Same line, same feet, Gopal." He's seventy now. Last month, on the phone, he admitted Green was probably the worst house for rules. Your Rukmini Paati still remembers that faded chalk.

qa.q: Which house was Gopal in?
qa.a: Gopal was Green House, heart and soul.

qa.q: Why did Gopal call it an accident for Green but cheating for Blue?
qa.a: He loved Green House so much that belonging bent his fairness; his own side's foul felt excusable and the other side's felt wicked.

qa.q: What could Aparna say to the cousin who is shouting at the TV?
qa.a: Aparna could borrow Amma's line and ask, 'Same tackle, same feet?' to help him see he judges the two teams differently.

qa.q: How did young Rukmini, in Blue House, experience Gopal's shouting?
qa.a: Rukmini felt her house was treated unfairly, so they fought all the way home, though now it is a fond memory. 🙂

grounding: A grandmother recalls her brother excusing his house's foul but calling the same act cheating by another house.

passage: Rain had been threatening all afternoon, and the house cricket final had to finish before the sky opened. Kamal, captain of Tagore House, was fielding at point when his own bowler, Nikhil, threw the ball instead of bowling it. Kamal clapped. "Great ball!" Four overs later, with thunder rumbling, Arohi of Raman House did exactly the same. Kamal flung down his cap. "That's a throw! Cheating! Umpire!" The PT sir raised an eyebrow. "Kamal, Nikhil's arm bent the same way." "That was different, sir. It was wet, the ball slipped." "And now?" Kamal opened his mouth. The first fat drops of rain fell, and everyone ran for the corridor, but Arohi looked back at him, arms folded, until he looked away.

qa.q: What did Kamal do when Arohi threw the ball?
qa.a: Kamal flung down his cap and shouted, 'That's a throw! Cheating! Umpire!'

qa.q: Why did Nikhil's throw seem fine to Kamal but Arohi's seem like cheating?
qa.a: As Tagore House captain, Kamal felt protective of his side and eager to win, so he found an excuse for Nikhil and none for the rival house.

qa.q: What could Kamal do after he looks away from Arohi?
qa.a: He could admit to PT sir and Arohi that both throws were the same, and use one rule for both houses.

qa.q: What might Arohi be thinking, arms folded, looking back at Kamal?
qa.a: Arohi probably thinks Kamal is being unfair, calling out the same action that Kamal clapped for from Tagore House.

grounding: A house captain cheers his own bowler's illegal throw and calls the same action cheating from a rival, as rain rushes the match.

passage: The inter-house kabaddi match in the school's concrete courtyard in Pune was the loudest event of the year. Yogesh, in Shivaji House, had painted his cheeks orange. When Shivaji's raider stepped out of bounds and kept going, Yogesh screamed, "He was in! He was in!" When the Tilak raider did the same a minute later, Yogesh was first to shout, "Out! Out! Cheat!" His classmate Swati, who was in Tilak and standing beside him, stared. "It's the same line, Yogesh." "Our raider was fast. The line is blurry there." "And ours?" "Yours was cheating." He said it with a grin, carried along by the chanting. On the bus home he noticed the orange paint on his fingers and didn't feel so sure any more.

qa.q: What colour had Yogesh painted his cheeks?
qa.a: Orange.

qa.q: Why does Yogesh say 'Our raider was fast. The line is blurry there'?
qa.a: Yogesh feels so excited and eager for his house to win that he finds excuses for Shivaji House while calling the same step cheating from Tilak.

qa.q: How could a teacher help students judge fairly during house matches?
qa.a: A teacher could replay both raids side by side and ask students to call them without knowing which house was which.

qa.q: How might Swati feel standing beside Yogesh?
qa.a: Swati may feel frustrated and a bit hurt that Swati's house is called cheats for the same step Yogesh defended.

grounding: A boy cheers his house's out-of-bounds raid but calls the same move by another house cheating.

passage:
"Foul! That's a foul!" Rafiq shouted, jumping up from the stands of the inter-house relay.
Jahnavi, beside him, raised an eyebrow. "Rafiq, Manas from your house did the exact same thing in the last race. He stepped into lane three."
"That wasn't a foul. He slipped. The track was wet."
"The track is still wet."
"But Neela from Red House did it on purpose. Look at her face."
"She's just tired."
Rafiq folded his arms. "You're only saying that because you're in Red House."
"And you're only saying the opposite because you're in Blue House."
He opened his mouth, then closed it. The next Blue House runner started early, and Rafiq cheered louder than anyone. Jahnavi just looked at him.
"What?" he said. "That was… a good start."

qa.q: Which lane did the Blue House runner step into, according to Jahnavi?
qa.a: He stepped into lane three.

qa.q: Why does Rafiq feel his own house's runner slipped but Red House's runner cheated?
qa.a: Rafiq feels protective of Blue House and wants his team to be good, so its mistakes feel like accidents while the same move by another house looks deliberate.

qa.q: What could Rafiq ask himself next time he's about to shout 'Foul!'?
qa.a: He could ask whether he'd call it a foul if his own house did it, the same question Jahnavi's point raised.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Rafiq's cheering at the early start?
qa.a: Jahnavi probably finds it both funny and frustrating, since he has just called the same kind of thing a foul when Red House did it.

grounding: It shows a schoolboy excusing his own house's fouls while calling the same acts cheating by another house, belonging bending his sense of fairness.

passage:
I'm Omkar, and in Class 6 I was the loudest boy in the Blue House stands. At the football match against Yellow House, I screamed "Handball!" every time a Yellow player's arm got near the ball. When our striker grabbed the ball with both hands, I told everyone, "It bounced up, it wasn't his fault."
After the match, my friend Tushar, who's in Yellow House, said, "Omkar, you're only fair when you're wearing blue."
I was angry. But on the walk home I kept thinking about our striker's hands. Tushar was right. Being in Blue House felt so good, I just wanted us to win.
Now, before I shout, I try to ask myself: would I call it the same if the shirt was a different colour? It's hard. I still cheer loudly. Just a bit less unfairly.

qa.q: What did Tushar tell Omkar after the match?
qa.a: Tushar said, "Omkar, you're only fair when you're wearing blue."

qa.q: Why did Omkar excuse his own striker's handball?
qa.a: Omkar felt proud and excited to be in Blue House and badly wanted them to win, so his own team's foul seemed like an accident while Yellow's looked like cheating.

qa.q: What question does Omkar now ask himself before shouting?
qa.a: He asks whether he would call it the same if the shirt was a different colour.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt watching Omkar shout 'Handball!' at Yellow House?
qa.a: Tushar probably felt annoyed and a bit hurt, since Tushar's house was being accused of what Blue House was also doing, which is why Tushar spoke up.

grounding: A boy recalls cheering his house unfairly and excusing its fouls while calling the same acts cheating by others, because belonging felt good.
